Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.text: The sum includes the potential budget, possible fitted-direction budgets and the free parameter and time-shift budgets. Setting the fitted set empty and adding the separate pin charge gives the three-part expression (B.53).
The flux is ∇ψ−ΣYⱼₗ(∇Φ̃ₗ−∇Φ̃ₗᵀ). For divergence-free generators its negative divergence gives −∆ψ+ΣYⱼₗ∆Φ̃ₗ, identifying the corresponding terms of (B.52).

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalBounded.text: The harmonic part has distinct component, time-frequency and azimuthal-frequency triples and the weighted sum with denominator (|k|+1/2)². This is exactly the improved harmonic budget in the definition preceding Lemma B.11.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti.text: The identity assumes L² matrix columns and |y| times their divergence in L². The paper states (B.55) for matrix fields with divergence in L⁶ᐟ⁵; these are different sufficient hypotheses, and the formal argument uses the weighted Hardy bound.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsPotentialData.text: The potential assumptions add $|U|\lesssim(1+|y|)^{-1}$ and require bounded-near-origin Laplacians with decay $(1+|y|)^{-4}$ for $G$ and $(1+|y|)^{-3}$ for $U$. These imply the coarser common derivative bound (B.51), after increasing its unspecified constant.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointDefectBri.text: The theorem combines the potential, parameter and pin estimates after decomposing the adjoint pairing. It concludes the absolute bound (7.33); the raw three-line equality (B.56) is established through separate identities inside that argument.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.remainderField.text: The residual combines the adjoint transport, negative divergence of the pin flux, ∇q, ∆G+w*∆U and −div Fᵀ. With divergence-free pin generators and the stated transpose convention, this is (B.52).

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.heightRat.text: For y≠0 the polar coordinate is y₃/|y|. A value is also assigned at y=0, where the polar coordinate in the paper is undefined; none of the geometric formulas needs that point.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CellSystemCond.text: The fifteen groups of assumptions include multiplier bounds, pointwise cell inequalities, matrix comparisons, and profile, potential, adjoint and offset conditions. They supply the full hypothesis of the certificate construction, including the requirements omitted after Proposition B.14; their satisfaction by concrete data remains an assumption.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isExtendedCert.text: The construction produces a certificate after choosing a sufficiently large decay constant, from the full fifteen groups of cell assumptions and the analytic estimates. The paper omits some finite-data hypotheses, so equivalence of the complete condition lists cannot be checked from Proposition B.14 alone.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.spaceBreakdown.text: The conclusion is whole-space nonexistence of a global smooth solution with uniformly bounded energy, obtained by composing the cell and profile implications. Proposition B.14 itself concludes that the data form a certificate; the existence of valid concrete data remains an assumption here.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is.text: The profile representation is linked to its derivatives and to pinning values, with the target chosen to equal the approximate profile's pinning values. Consequently the correction has the zero pinning gap prescribed in Appendix B; the general certificate of Section 7 allows other gaps.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.FreePerturbation.text: The free similarity equation is verified by differentiating its pairing with smooth compactly supported test fields.

Breakdown.Cert.bordered.text: The unknown is $f = T_S v$; applying the free inverse recovers $v$ before convection and the constraints are evaluated.

Breakdown.Cert.extendedDataContinuityHol.text: Continuity is proved after testing the residual against solenoidal fields. No continuity of the unprojected residual in H is assumed.

Breakdown.Cert.extendedFrozenBridgeHolds.text: The lower bound at the approximate profile is obtained by adding the reference-profile lower bound and the allowed shift of the quadratic form.

Breakdown.Cert.freeEnergyLocalHolds_of.text: The energy identity is integrated over time intervals for a continuous periodic scalar energy. The physical-time identity (7.45) is related by the similarity change of variables.

Breakdown.Cert.productBoundHolds_of.text: The estimate allows different first and second factors, using the weighted norm of the first and the gradient supremum of the second.

Breakdown.Cert.sizeZ.text: At this stage ω has been reduced to one by rescaling the forcing fields and their coefficients.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.EliminationC.text: The cell-matrix comparison is imposed on the allowed local vectors, with further eliminated-mode and row-matrix conditions. Identifying that set with the vectors XQxg also uses the pressure-gauge and compatibility conditions omitted from the paper.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.InRowRange.text: A compatible local vector is a global row value plus pressure-gauge and constant-pressure directions, with real forcing and pinning coordinates. This is more explicit than the paper's notation x=XQxg, and the equivalence uses the additional gauge-invariance conditions.

Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.Internal.ModeT.text: The gradient-coefficient reflection identity is proved for y₃≠0. This is sufficient for the integrated symmetry argument, while the printed (B.17) is written without the pointwise restriction.
The curl-coefficient reflection identity is proved for y₃≠0. The printed (B.17) gives no such exclusion; the excluded plane has zero measure for the density integrals.
The velocity-coefficient reflection identity is proved for y₃≠0. The restriction leaves the integral unchanged but is narrower than the unrestricted pointwise wording of (B.17).
The curl-gradient allocation is invariant under the reflected label and point when y₃≠0. The printed coefficient identity does not state this restriction.

Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.IsFlipCompatib.text: The weight and harmonic reflection conditions are explicit, while reflection of the auxiliary piecewise constant functions is required only off y₃=0. Thus the complete pointwise hypothesis differs from the unrestricted wording preceding (B.17).

Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.IsModeClass.text: The two required symmetries are the half-period twist by π/κ and the half-turn about the first axis. The auxiliary condition allows κ≥1; the cell assumptions impose the paper's κ≥3.

Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.modeFlip.text: The reflected velocity-mode identity is proved almost everywhere for weak perturbations, together with the corresponding gradient and Hessian identities. The velocity clause is (B.24), interpreted in the weak-function setting of the surrounding argument.

Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.modeShiftRotat.text: For periodic fields whose orbital integral exists, a time shift and axial rotation multiply the projected mode by its harmonic and rotate its vector value. This is (B.13), with the integrability needed for the change of variables stated explicitly.

Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.modeTermFlip.text: The density reflection identity follows from the coefficient and derivative reflection identities at points with y₃≠0. It provides the almost-everywhere equality needed in the integrals, with a pointwise restriction absent from (B.17).

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsCellFo.text: The local inequality uses explicit row, pairing, strain-slack and credit contributions and separates the positive and negative integrals. It serves the role of (B.33), with a specified symmetric pressure gradient and without the paper's four existential error variables.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellHypothesis.text: The full cell assumptions include $\kappa\ge 3$ and the constants $w^*=39/50$, $c=3/50$, pinning weight $1000$ and row cap $400(1+2^{-18})$. They also require the cell, matrix, pressure and error conditions described, and partly omitted, in Appendix B.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.field.text: The cell tensor has the same harmonic and reflection construction as Ξᵢ, with matrix indices ordered as output then derivative direction. Transposing the paper's derivative-first convention identifies the same pairing in (B.10).

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesCom.text: The complex-node condition includes the two comparisons and weighted residual test, together with the permitted complex coordinates, scale, pivot bounds and real and imaginary negative columns. These are the additional conditions described after (B.40).

Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel.text: These are the conjugation, reflection, spline joining, vanishing and exponent conditions around (B.6)–(B.8). They specify admissible coefficients; the vector-field formula itself is supplied separately.

Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.reducedCom.text: The nonzero azimuthal mode uses the factors σʰ⁰(1−σ)ʰ(1−η²)² and division by κι₁ to enforce zero divergence. The zero azimuthal mode uses the stream and swirl formulas of (B.8).

Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.shapeInfoF.text: The represented field is the real part of the finite vector-harmonic sum, as printed in (B.6). Conjugation, reflection and spline matching are required separately.

Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.GeneratedByC.text: Every allowed symmetry is a power of the axial twist, possibly followed by the half-turn, with an integer time translation. This is the restriction on Γ stated after (B.1).

Breakdown.CertCell.ModeCoefficients.ofPi.text: The five cell coefficients include the leading terms printed below (B.16) and the full multiplier corrections. The paper explicitly leaves those corrections unwritten, so their complete formulas cannot be compared term by term with the manuscript.

Breakdown.CertCell.RowValues.mix.text: For positive definite Gram data the mixing matrix is $G^{-1/2}$. The factor $\sqrt{\tau_k}$ is applied through the separate row weight when the row seminorm is formed.

Breakdown.CertCell.RowValues.rowFieldOf.text: The formal row fields have unit norm after multiplication by $G^{-1/2}$. The paper includes $\sqrt{\tau_k}$ in $e_k$ itself; the same seminorm is recovered by multiplying the squared formal row pairing by $\tau_k$.

Breakdown.CertCell.RowValues.rowWeightOf.text: The row weight is the cell test weight divided by $c$; at $c=3/50$ it is $\tau_k$. The paper places $\sqrt{\tau_k}$ in the field $e_k$, whereas the formal row seminorm carries $\tau_k$ as a separate weight.

Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsDirectionR.text: The directional radius is measurable, homogeneous of degree zero, uniformly positive and bounded above. The paper allows dependence on direction without spelling out these uniform bounds.

Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.TailBudget.H.text: The complete absorption condition bounds the sum of gradient, potential, leakage and velocity-tail charges by I₂ times the gain in (B.27). The printed expression specifies the available threshold, without listing every charge in this condition.

Breakdown.CertCell.initialState_closed.text: The global estimate already uses 2ζ·ℓ−|ζ|²/1000≤1000|ℓ|². It therefore bounds the assembled form by the final density gap, while (B.44) still displays the uncompleted pinning square.

Breakdown.CertCell.labelPhase.text: The harmonic is exp(i[2π(2ι₂−ι₁)θ+κι₁φ]), with the same signs and integer frequencies as (B.2).

Breakdown.CertReduction.EnergyBoundsHold.text: The combined assertion consists of spatial supremum and period energy estimates at constant weight. The paper's (B.46) is a four-part spatial statement assuming only a lower bound for a possibly variable weight.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.IsAdmissibleWeak.text: Admissibility includes positive c,cμ<1, a positive period and lower weight, regularity and decay, transport and harmonic bounds, one-sided frequencies and all auxiliary losses. The paper describes several of these requirements without writing their complete formulas.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.PieceMultiplierDe.text: This is the full multiplier assertion for weak perturbations, with positive and negative density integrals kept separate. It yields the real signed inequality of Proposition B.1 once the negative part is finite and the full coefficient assumptions hold.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.RowRestClause.text: The condition states finiteness of negative density and the lower bound (B.21), with c and the pinning weight as parameters. Taking c=3/50 and the pinning weight 1000 gives the printed constants, after subtracting the finite negative integral.

Breakdown.DichotomyHolds.text: For a compact perturbation of an operator of norm at most b≤α<β, the spectral conclusion gives a commuting finite-rank projection and geometric bounds with α<r₁<r₂<β, together with surjectivity on the exceptional range. Taking α=b=exp(−S/4), β=1 and r₁<Θ<r₂ gives the two convergent series in (4.11).

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.IsHeld.text: A fixed-parameter correction must satisfy the equation, constraints, weighted radius and essential gradient-supremum bound.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.defect.text: A weak Hessian and a pressure-gradient representative are selected when the residual field is formed.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.params.text: Intervals constrain the adjoint coordinates; a scaled Euclidean ball constrains the complementary coordinates.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.target.text: Subtract the approximate profile’s constraint from the complete-field target to obtain the prescribed correction target ℓ̄(α).

Breakdown.FarField.farFieldDecay_holds.text: Weighted estimates for the profile integral equation give velocity derivatives through order two and pressure-gradient decay.

Breakdown.FarField.periodicLerayProfileE.text: The input and output assert existence. The conclusion does not preserve an equality with a specified original weak field.

Breakdown.FarField.smoothFieldOfOrbit_ho.text: The smooth velocity preserves the chosen mild orbit at every time, with equality almost everywhere in space.

Breakdown.Freq.BilinCompact.text: For positive heat time, the operator in the second input is compact when its first input is a compact smooth solenoidal field in the dense test class. Lemma 3.2 allows every first input in X; extending to that class uses density and continuity in operator norm.

Breakdown.Freq.IsWeakSolution.text: The weak momentum identity is imposed at interior times against compact solenoidal test fields, with diffusion written by the gradient pairing and transport by the advection pairing. The full assumptions also require smooth decaying slices, continuity in X, L²-continuous differences between slices, and continuity of test pairings at the endpoints.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinX.text: The bilinear operator on X is specified by its dual trilinear pairing, with the transport formula then proved on a dense compact test class. Display (2.3) defines it through projected heat evolution for all inputs in X.

Breakdown.Freq.heatDivFree.text: The projected heat map takes L² forcing into the gradient-weighted Fourier realization of X. The formula in (2.2) is stated on the larger class L¹+L².

Breakdown.HeatBilinear.text: The heat operators form a strongly continuous contraction semigroup, and the symmetric bilinear kernel commutes with forward heat shifts. Its $\tau^{-3/4}$ bound is required only for $0<\tau\le 1$, whereas (3.12) requires that bound for every $\tau>0$.

Breakdown.Held.testSetZero_of.text: The proof forms the simplified Newton update and uses the two enclosures to keep it in K; a fixed point then has zero total force.

Breakdown.IsPerturbation.text: The drift-time field is $S^{-1}\partial_\theta v + \frac{1}{2}v + \frac{1}{2}(y\cdot\nabla)v$. The Laplacian is subtracted separately in the equation.

Breakdown.IsRightSide.text: The relation is equality of integrals against all smooth compactly supported solenoidal space-time tests.

Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile.text: The velocity and pressure solve the smooth similarity equation, with $|\nabla^j W| \le C(1+|y|)^{-1-j}$ for $j=0,1,2$ and $|\nabla q| \le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$. Periodicity and nonvanishing are separate assumptions when this local profile condition is used.

Breakdown.IsSmoothSolution.text: The velocity and pressure are smooth on nonnegative times, the prescribed initial velocity is attained, and the momentum equation and zero divergence hold at positive times. Setting the viscosity to one gives (1.1).

Breakdown.MildFramework.IsOrbit.text: A continuous nonzero energy-space curve has positive period P, obeys w(s+P)=ρw(s), and solves the similarity-time integral equation. The physical-time identities (1.5) and (4.2) require the change of variables and dilation as well.

Breakdown.MildRegular.text: From compact smooth solenoidal initial data, a mild curve on [0,T] has smooth velocity and pressure representatives, with bounded kinetic energy and gradient norm on that interval. Lemma 2.3 additionally states energy nonincrease throughout the lifespan and a periodic assertion.

Breakdown.MonodromyStatement.text: After sufficiently short intervals are composed and the twist removed, the period map differs compactly from the free product, whose norm is at most exp(−P/4). The same statement also provides inverses of the short-interval operators with norm at most 4/3.

Breakdown.Periodic.HeatDivFreeComparison.text: Compactly supported $L^2$ forcing has arbitrarily small local projected-heat discrepancy, measured by $\delta$ times its $L^{3/2}$ norm, at sufficiently small scale and on a compact positive-time window. Lemma 6.1 gives an all-time $CL^{-7/2}$ estimate for the divergence of a $W^{1,1}$ tensor, in terms of that tensor’s $L^1$ norm.

Breakdown.Periodic.KernelSharpBound.text: The bilinear smoothing bound is $C\tau^{-3/4}$ in the inhomogeneous unit-torus norm, for $0<\tau\le 1$. Lemma 3.7 and (3.20) use mean-zero homogeneous spaces at every spatial period and all positive times.

Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup.text: The conclusion supplies a smooth periodic solenoidal datum and a mild trajectory whose inhomogeneous H¹ norm is unbounded on [0,T), for some T>0. Proposition 2.2 additionally gives T≤1, the two-sided rate, and local convergence to the profile.

Breakdown.Periodic.TransplantNorm.text: The rescaled transplant has squared norm ∫|∇g|²+μ∫|g|² because the unit-torus norm is inhomogeneous. The equality in (6.1) concerns the homogeneous gradient norm, preserved by unscaled periodization.

Breakdown.Periodic.V.text: The unit-torus Fourier norm uses 1+4π²|k|² and permits the zero mode. Displays (3.15) and (3.16) concern the homogeneous gradient norm on mean-zero fields, with a separate equivalence to H¹ at period one.

Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist.text: A smooth nonzero profile has a positive period and an orthogonal twist, solves the similarity equation, and satisfies uniform bounds $|\nabla^j W| \le C(1+|y|)^{-1-j}$ for $j=0,1,2$ and $|\nabla q| \le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$. The second-derivative and pressure-gradient bounds are additional written hypotheses beyond (1.3).

Breakdown.PieceWeights.IsMultiplierField.text: The multiplier is characterized by the test pairing in (B.14), with finite L² norm, time periodicity and zero pairing against pressure gradients. These are the stated requirements that Mv belong to Hdiv.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.IsPotentialSeri.text: The condition imposes polynomial joining, axis behavior and endpoint decay for the finite potential series. The paper explicitly does not print that representation, so this condition cannot be identified with the displayed analytic bounds (B.51) alone.

Breakdown.TransferHolds.text: For every prescribed dense class of initial data and every ε>0, the formal conclusion chooses one mild solution whose datum is within ε of W(0) and whose dilated error is at most C(1−t)^κ for some κ>0. Proposition 2.1 also chooses a fixed finite-dimensional correction space and treats every sufficiently close datum; that whole family is absent from this conclusion.

Breakdown.WeakProfile.physicalCurve.text: The formula uses s = s₀ − log(1−t) and dilation by 1/(1−t); conversion from normalized time θ to s has already occurred.

Breakdown.WeakProfile.physicalIdentity_o.text: The theorem transforms the weak nonlinear equation after testing. The paper also interprets the separate free-operator identities (7.41) distributionally.

Breakdown.extended_certificate_orbit_pro.text: The proof assembles the analytic implications, while its conclusion retains only existence of a weak profile. The parameter and quantitative bounds are not part of that conclusion.

Breakdown.physicalField.text: The physical curve is $D_{(1-t)^{-1}}W(s_0-\log(1-t))$, with final time fixed to one and arbitrary phase $s_0$. Display (1.4) allows any positive final time $T$.

Breakdown.rowNorm.text: The weights of orthonormal row fields can be absorbed into the fields to recover the paper’s orthogonal family.

Breakdown.sigmaSimilarityIntegrand.text: Solenoidal tests remove pressure, and integration by parts transfers the derivatives to the test field.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou.text: The condition collects all potential, remainder, parameter and pin-error bounds and their final sum. It allows fitted directions; after setting that set empty, its numerical budget is (B.53), while the implication to (7.33) is a separate theorem.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.text: This is the adjoint transport evaluated at the central period and central profile. The Laplacian, pin flux and potential corrections of Rⱼ,α in (B.52) are not part of this expression.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalBounded.text: The harmonic part has distinct component, time-frequency and azimuthal-frequency triples and the weighted sum with denominator (|k|+1/2)². This is exactly the improved harmonic budget in the definition preceding Lemma B.11.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.m.text: The weak extension controls a sum of projected modes using the sharp inverse-square factors and the total gradient energy. Breakdown.MildFramework.IsMildOn.text: A continuous curve satisfies the heat-plus-quadratic Duhamel equation on [a,b), with convergence of each time integral. This is precisely the mild-solution condition surrounding (2.4).

Breakdown.MildFramework.IsOrbit.text: A continuous nonzero energy-space curve has positive period P, obeys w(s+P)=ρw(s), and solves the similarity-time integral equation. The physical-time identities (1.5) and (4.2) require the change of variables and dilation as well.

Breakdown.MildFramework.gluePieces.text: Successive rescaled compact time intervals are joined by undoing their dilations. The weighted global Cκ norm in (4.5) is represented through the bounds on these intervals and is not the object defined here.

Breakdown.MildFramework.profilePiece.text: The nth short interval is the physical curve with similarity-time phase nP/k, restricted to its compact interval. The four normalized perturbation and forcing quantities in (4.13) are different objects.

Breakdown.MildFramework.selfSimilar.text: The physical curve is $D_{(1-t)^{-1}}W(s_0-\log(1-t))$, with final time fixed to one and arbitrary phase $s_0$. Display (1.4) allows any positive final time $T$.

Breakdown.MildFramework.stepOp.text: On one short rescaled interval, the linearized interaction is v↦2B(u*,v). Solving the equation in (4.9) also requires inversion of I−2B(u*,·) and subsequent heat evolution of the datum.

Breakdown.MildRegular.text: From compact smooth solenoidal initial data, a mild curve on [0,T] has smooth velocity and pressure representatives, with bounded kinetic energy and gradient norm on that interval. Lemma 2.3 additionally states energy nonincrease throughout the lifespan and a periodic assertion.

Breakdown.MonodromyStatement.text: After sufficiently short intervals are composed and the twist removed, the period map differs compactly from the free product, whose norm is at most exp(−P/4). The same statement also provides inverses of the short-interval operators with norm at most 4/3.

Breakdown.Periodic.AdvectShellBounds.text: For a compact smooth solenoidal field $\phi$ and local perturbation data $\zeta$, the localized transport is supported in the chosen ball and has $L^{3/2}$ norm at most $C\lVert\phi\rVert_X\lVert\zeta\rVert$. The time-dependent factor $(1-t)^{-1/4}$ in (6.8) comes from a separate bound on the profile.

Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxFieldProperties.text: The smooth solenoidal cutoff has fixed support around the centre of the unit torus and agrees exactly with the physical profile on a fixed inner ball. Lemma 5.1 uses an arbitrary radius r and additionally gives explicit gradient-error and mass estimates.

Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxResidualSmall.text: For the normalized $n$th approximate interval, the residual is bounded by $\theta^n KT^{1/4}$, assuming the profile bounds and $\lambda^{1/4}<\theta$. Lemma 6.2 instead states a global $C^\kappa$ residual bound of order $L^{-1/2}$ on the large torus.

Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxSizes.text: For sufficiently small positive final time, the normalized approximate intervals have a uniform upper bound and pointwise lower norm bound c/2. This does not itself assert a norm identity under periodization or a rate for the corrected trajectory.

Breakdown.Periodic.ComparisonSmall.text: For any δ>0, the localized interaction and initial-data maps on the unit torus are within δ of their whole-space counterparts when the scale is sufficiently small. The statement gives no explicit power of the large period L in (6.11) or (6.15).

Breakdown.Periodic.FreeHeatComparison.text: For each compact smooth solenoidal datum, the rescaled torus and whole-space free heat flows converge uniformly on a bounded nonnegative time interval as the scale tends to zero. Display (6.3) gives the explicit all-positive-time error $CL^{-5/2}\lVert f\rVert_{L^1}$.

Breakdown.Periodic.GlueUnbounded.text: A uniformly positive approximate norm and a bounded correction multiplied by θⁿ, with 0<θ<1, make the joined physical trajectory unbounded before its positive final time. The conclusion does not contain the all-time two-sided rate or the local comparison in (1.7).

Breakdown.Periodic.HeatDivFreeComparison.text: Compactly supported $L^2$ forcing has arbitrarily small local projected-heat discrepancy, measured by $\delta$ times its $L^{3/2}$ norm, at sufficiently small scale and on a compact positive-time window. Breakdown.Periodic.KernelSharpBound.text: The bilinear smoothing bound is $C\tau^{-3/4}$ in the inhomogeneous unit-torus norm, for $0<\tau\le 1$. Lemma 3.7 and (3.20) use mean-zero homogeneous spaces at every spatial period and all positive times.

Breakdown.Periodic.R3Factor.text: With one compact smooth solenoidal input, the whole-space bilinear interaction factors through the velocity and gradient restricted to its support ball. Time integration and assembly produce the first factorization in (6.9).

Proposition 4.1 also bundles nonvanishing and discrete self-similarity on [0,1).

Breakdown.pieceOperator.text: On [0,T], the bilinear Duhamel operator is bounded by 4C_K T¹⁄⁴ for T≤1, and the free heat-evolution operator has norm at most one. Lemma 4.7 expresses different, global Cκ estimates on [0,1).

Breakdown.piecePerturbation.text: On a compact interval of length at most one, a perturbation satisfying the linear-plus-quadratic equation has the given initial value and makes the sum an exact mild solution. Display (4.7) states both implications on the whole half-open lifespan.

Breakdown.pinValue.text: The functional integrates ∇v:Ξ_i over space and one unit time period, exactly ℓ_i(v) in (7.11). The matrix contraction uses the same Euclidean pairing after transposing the gradient convention consistently.

Breakdown.profilePiece.text: The rescaled profile intervals are mild, have matching dilated endpoints, recur under the twist every k intervals, and have a uniform upper bound inherited from the similarity orbit. The two-sided physical rate in Lemma 4.2 also uses the lower orbit bound and dilation law.

Breakdown.pushForward.text: The orthogonal action is $\rho_R u(x)=Ru(R^{-1}x)$, exactly as in (3.4), including reflections.

Breakdown.restrict.text: The quadratic mild equation can be restarted from any intermediate time by the heat semigroup law and adjacent-interval integration. Lemma 3.5 and (3.13) allow independent continuous factors f and h in the forcing, a larger class than the quadratic choice f=h=u.

Breakdown.rowNorm.text: The weighted Euclidean norm of pairings with orthonormal fields represents the paper’s unweighted norm of pairings with orthogonal fields. Absorbing $\sqrt{\tau_j}$ into the $j$th field identifies the quantities, while the supplied field normalization differs.

Breakdown.sigmaSimilarityIntegrand.text: The expression is the similarity equation tested against a solenoidal space-time field, with time coefficient 1/S and the spatial derivatives transferred by integration by parts. Pressure disappears from this weak equation, while (7.1) displays it explicitly.

Breakdown.sixthPowerGradientBound_four_t.text: The theorem states $\lVert u\rVert_{L^6}^2\le(4/3)\lVert\nabla u\rVert_{L^2}^2$ for an $L^6$ field with $L^2$ weak gradient. Taking square roots gives (B.45) with constant $2/\sqrt{3}$.

Breakdown.stationaryEnergy.text: The one-time energy is ∫|Δu|² + ∫w|∇u|², exactly |u|²_w in (7.14). The forcing-coefficient weight ω belongs to the separate norm of a pair.

Breakdown.stepData.text: The right inverse acts on bounded sequences of short rescaled time intervals, returns an exceptional coordinate in a fixed finite-dimensional space, and lifts its initial correction into the chosen dense class. Proposition 4.3 writes the corresponding problem as one trajectory in Cκ([0,1);X).

Breakdown.stepMap.text: A short-interval step sends initial data through free evolution, the inverse of the interval linearization, and endpoint evaluation. The monodromy in (4.10) composes all such steps in a period and removes the twist.

Breakdown.stretchForm.text: The stretching expression has the negative strain-curl square, the vorticity-gradient coupling and the final cross-product term with coefficient 1/2. Its signs and contractions agree with (B.18).

Breakdown.supBoundFactor.text: The constant simplifies to $(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$, exactly $c_w$ in (7.15), when $w_* > 0$.

Breakdown.transferHolds_of_dichotomy.text: For every prescribed dense class of initial data and every ε>0, the formal conclusion chooses one mild solution whose datum is within ε of W(0) and whose dilated error is at most C(1−t)^κ for some κ>0. Proposition 2.1 also chooses a fixed finite-dimensional correction space and treats every sufficiently close datum; that whole family is absent from this conclusion.

Breakdown.varConstIntegral.text: For two continuous curves on any compact interval, the Duhamel integral exists and is continuous up to both endpoints. The formal statement adds the estimate 4C_K(t−a)¹⁄⁴MN when t−a≤1, with M and N bounds for the input curves.

Breakdown.weakDefectField.text: The expression includes $T_S W$, convection, forcing and a supplied pressure-gradient field, with the Laplacian given by a chosen weak Hessian. Setting the forcing to zero and identifying that Hessian and pressure gradient recovers the strong expression in (7.1).

Breakdown.weightedEnergy.text: The energy is ∫₀¹∫(|Δv|² + w|∇v|²), exactly ‖v‖²_w in (7.14) on the admissible finite-energy class. It contains no forcing-coefficient term.

Breakdown.FarField.heatConv.text: The displayed integral is convolution with the Gaussian heat kernel. It describes the positive-time formula in (2.1); the identity at time zero is supplied by the heat semigroup, separately.

Breakdown.FarField.HeatVelocity.text: For positive time, the reconstructed velocity of the heat evolution equals Gaussian convolution almost everywhere for each element of X. Display (2.1) defines heat evolution on every Lᵖ space, including the identity convention at time zero.
